body: {"total":6,"records":[{"title":"Peer support for people with early psychosis: a systematic review","authors":"Kinsella-Obi R, Marchand-Asante L, Petrova-Hale D","year":2020,"venue":"Early Intervention in Mental Health Reviews","doi":"10.5555/eimhr.2020.0152","providerType":"review","abstract":"We included nine studies of peer support for people within five years of a first episode of psychosis, two of them randomised. Peer support was associated with better engagement with services and higher scores on hope and recovery measures, but there was no clear effect on readmission or symptoms. Definitions of the peer role varied widely, from one-to-one mentoring to group facilitation, and few studies described training or supervision. Most studies were small and short, and only three reported how many eligible people took up the offer."},{"title":"Peer support workers in early intervention services for psychosis: a randomised feasibility trial","authors":"Adeyemi-Lindqvist S, Harcourt-Nakamura J, Osei-Brennan T","year":2022,"venue":"Journal of Psychosis Services Research","doi":"10.5555/jpsr.2022.0088","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"In two early intervention teams we aimed to randomise 80 young people to peer support plus usual care or usual care alone over 12 months. We recruited 64 participants, and 78 percent provided six-month outcome data. Participants allocated to peer support had a median of 1.8 contacts a week with their peer worker. Recovery questionnaires were completed by 70 percent at six months, lower among participants under 18. The trial met its progression criteria for recruitment and retention and was judged feasible for a definitive trial."},{"title":"Role clarity, supervision and turnover among peer support workers in community mental health teams: a mixed-methods study","authors":"Fairclough-Mbatha E, Olsen-Achebe K","year":2019,"venue":"Mental Health Workforce Studies","doi":"10.5555/mhws.2019.0041","providerType":"mixed methods study","abstract":"We surveyed 118 peer support workers and interviewed 24 in community mental health teams. Forty percent of those surveyed had left their post within a year, most often citing unclear roles, being asked to do administrative work and lack of supervision from someone with lived experience. Workers with protected supervision and a written role description stayed longer. Several described distress when working with people whose experiences echoed their own. The study was cross-sectional, so causes of turnover cannot be separated from features of the teams."},{"title":"Disengagement from early intervention in psychosis services: rates and predictors in a regional cohort","authors":"Brennan-Oduya M, Tavares-Holm J","year":2017,"venue":"Psychosis Services Quarterly","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Among 1,102 young people accepted by four early intervention services, 23 percent disengaged within 12 months, defined as no contact for three months despite attempts. Disengagement was more common among young men, people using cannabis daily and people without stable housing, and less common when a family member was involved in care. Most disengagement happened in the first six months. Reasons were recorded for only a third of those who disengaged, and the study could not assess which service features protected against it."},{"title":"What young people and families want from peer support in early psychosis: interviews in three services","authors":"Achterberg-Sesay F, Moreno-Whitfield A","year":2023,"venue":"Journal of Psychosis Services Research","doi":"10.5555/jpsr.2023.0211","providerType":"qualitative research","abstract":"We interviewed 27 young people and 14 family members from three early intervention services. Young people valued meeting someone who had lived through psychosis and come out the other side, and preferred flexible contact by text or in community places rather than clinic rooms. Families welcomed practical advice on navigating services. Some young people worried that a peer worker would pass information to the clinical team, and some families felt excluded when contact was one-to-one. Participants asked for clear rules on confidentiality before starting."},{"title":"Brief recovery and hope questionnaires in early psychosis: completion rates and responsiveness","authors":"Lindahl-Okonkwo P, Saraswat-Doyle C","year":2024,"venue":"Outcome Measurement in Mental Health","doi":"10.5555/ommh.2024.0019","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We examined completion and responsiveness of three brief recovery and hope questionnaires given at routine reviews in early intervention services. Completion was 74 percent at baseline and 58 percent at six months, lowest among young people under 18 and those who had missed reviews. The shortest questionnaire was completed most often and detected change as well as the longer ones. Completion rose when a named worker asked in person rather than by post. We recommend the shortest questionnaire for routine use."}]}
